My values are w=$71, x=$47, y=$71, z=$77. My ranking at each school is w:1, x:2, y:1, z:2. Most applicants favor y > x > w > z.

If I rank y first, and get rejected, I'll go to w. My ranking at w is 1, so I'll likely get in. If I then get rejected from w (unlikely, but possible), I'll go to z. My ranking at z is 2, which isn't great, but z is valued at $77, which is the highest of all schools.

If I rank w first, and get rejected, I'll go to y. My ranking at y is 1, so I'll likely get in. If I then get rejected from y (possible, given its popularity), I'll go to z. My ranking at z is 2, and it's valued at $77.

Given that most applicants favor y > x > w > z, and I have a good ranking at w (1), I believe ranking w first gives me a better chance of ending up with a good outcome. If y is saturated, w is a solid backup. If I rank y first and it doesn't work out, my backup w could also be full.

Therefore, I will rank w first, then y, then z, and finally x. This strategy aims to secure a high-value school (w or y) and have a reasonable fallback option (z) with a decent value. X is the least desirable option given my values and the general applicant preference.
